title: Splunk
summary: Splunk is a third-party commercial platform for collecting, indexing and searching machine data, and it is one of the most common back ends for a security operations centre. This page is an independent study resource; it is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by Splunk. The mechanism is a pipeline. Universal and heavy forwarders read logs on hosts and send them to indexers, which break the stream into events, assign each event a timestamp and a host, source and sourcetype, and write it into a time-ordered index. Search heads then run the Search Processing Language (SPL) across those indexes as a distributed job: a base search retrieves raw events, and piped commands such as stats, eval, lookup, transaction and tstats transform, enrich and aggregate them. Knowledge objects - field extractions, calculated fields, event types, tags, lookups and the common information model - decide whether those fields are consistent across product families, or whether every search has to reinvent its own parsing. Scheduled searches and correlation searches turn that language into recurring detections, and their results feed alert queues or a notable event framework. The mistake practitioners make most often is treating ingestion as the finished job: data arrives, so it is assumed to be searchable and correctly parsed, when in truth an unextracted field silently breaks every detection that depends on it. Other recurring faults are searches with no time bounds, cardinality explosions from stats on raw fields, duplicate events replayed by a forwarder, and content that is measured by search cost only after it has already saturated the licence.

beginner.definition: Splunk is a software platform that collects computer records and makes them searchable. It is a third-party product, and this page is an independent study page. Companies use it to find problems in their systems. The records it stores are called logs (automatic notes that computers write about what they did).
beginner.whyItMatters: Computers write huge amounts of notes every minute. Reading all of those notes by hand is simply impossible. If you cannot search them, you cannot see an attack in progress. Splunk turns those notes into answers that you can act on quickly. Without a tool like this, a team may miss the evidence of what happened.
howItWorks: Small agents on your computers and servers forward their notes to the central Splunk platform.
The platform reads each note, gives it a time and a source, and stores it in a searchable index.
You then write a search that filters those notes and shows the events you care about.
Extra steps in the search can count, group and compare events across many different systems.
You can save a search to run on a schedule and raise an alert when it finds a match.
Analysts review those alerts, keep notes, and mark each one as real or harmless.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital where every nurse and doctor writes a short note about each patient. The notes pile up in hundreds of drawers across the building. When a patient becomes very ill, the night doctor needs to know what happened during the last two days. Reading every drawer by hand is completely impossible. So the hospital copies each note into one large index, sorted by patient, time and room. Now the doctor types a name and a date range, and the answer appears in seconds. Splunk does this with computer logs instead of patient notes.
takeaways: A search platform is only as useful as the notes that you send it.
Plan the fields you will need before an incident, not during one.
Splunk is a third-party product, so this page is independent study material.

objectives: Explain how forwarders, indexers and search heads divide the work of collecting, storing and searching machine data.
Describe how a Splunk search processes events in stages, and why the order of those stages changes both cost and results.
Identify which knowledge objects are needed to turn a raw log source into consistently named, reusable fields.
Explain how scheduled searches, alert actions and notable events connect detection content to an analyst queue.
Recognise common failure modes, including unparsed sources, duplicate events and searches with no time bounds.
Evaluate the search cost and schedule of a detection against the investigative value it returns.
